content: 1. Prolonged sedentary behavior is associated with increased risks of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, cancer mortality, and the incidence of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. 2. There is low to moderate certainty evidence suggesting that greater time spent in sedentary behavior is linked to a higher risk of developing endometrial, colon, and lung cancers. 3. Current evidence is insufficient to establish a clear association between sedentary behavior and measures of adiposity, necessitating further research. 4. The benefits of reducing sedentary behavior outweigh any potential risks. 5. Moderate certainty evidence indicates a non-linear dose-response relationship between sedentary time (measured via self-reported sitting or television viewing time, or device-based assessments) and adverse health outcomes, including all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, cancer mortality, and incident cardiovascular disease. 6. A recent meta-analysis with high certainty evidence demonstrated that increased sedentary time, as measured by accelerometers, is significantly associated with higher all-cause mortality, even after adjusting for confounding factors such as time spent in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity. 7. Evidence supports minimizing sedentary time to reduce health risks, although variations in assessment methods and thresholds for sedentary time across different health outcomes and population subgroups make it challenging to establish specific time-based recommendations. 8. Limited evidence exists to provide guidance on the frequency and duration of breaks in sedentary behavior. 9. Some types of sedentary behavior, such as television viewing, may have stronger associations with adverse health outcomes compared to total sitting time, potentially due to measurement errors or residual confounding in self-reported data. 10. Higher levels of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity can mitigate the negative health effects of sedentary behavior, with evidence showing that 60–75 minutes of such activity per day can attenuate or even eliminate the detrimental associations. 11. For older adults, regular physical activity improves all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, mental health, cognitive health, sleep, and physical function, while also reducing the risk of falls, fall-related injuries, and declines in bone health. 12. Older adults should engage in at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity, or an equivalent combination weekly for substantial health benefits. 13. Muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups should be performed on two or more days per week to provide additional health benefits. 14. Multicomponent physical activity programs emphasizing balance, strength, and functional training should be performed on three or more days per week to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. 15. Evidence shows an inverse dose-response relationship between the volume of aerobic physical activity and the risk of physical functional limitations in older adults, with more frequent and longer durations of activity associated with greater benefits. 16. Physical activity programs combining balance, strength, endurance, and gait training are effective in reducing the rate of falls and the risk of fall-related injuries in older adults. 17. Regular physical activity improves physical function and reduces the risk of age-related physical decline, including conditions such as sarcopenia and osteoporosis. 18. Higher levels of physical activity are recommended for individuals with high levels of sedentary behavior, as the benefits of physical activity outweigh the risks. 19. Doing some physical activity is better than doing none, and older adults should start with small amounts and gradually increase the frequency, intensity, and duration over time. 20. Future research using harmonized reporting and methods that distinguish between different types of sedentary behavior will strengthen the understanding of sedentary behavior patterns and their health impacts.
